lesson.title: The Sound of Nothing: Thermal Noise in Every Resistor
lesson.summary: Thermal noise, also called Johnson-Nyquist noise, is a random voltage generated by the thermal motion of electrons inside any resistance, and it sets a hard physical floor under every circuit's performance.
lesson.body:
Take a resistor, connect nothing to it, apply no voltage, and put it on a bench. If you could listen closely enough with a sensitive enough amplifier, you would still hear a faint, random hiss coming from its terminals. That hiss is thermal noise. It is not a flaw in the resistor or evidence of a bad component. It is a direct physical consequence of the resistor having some resistance and existing at a temperature above absolute zero. The free electrons inside the resistive material are in constant, random thermal motion, and that random jostling of charge produces a tiny, randomly fluctuating voltage across the resistor's leads. Every resistor you have studied, no matter how well made, does this.

The voltage is described by the Johnson-Nyquist noise formula: Vn (RMS) = sqrt(4 times k times T times R times B). Here k is Boltzmann's constant, about 1.38 times 10 to the negative 23 joules per kelvin, T is the absolute temperature in kelvin, R is the resistance in ohms, and B is the bandwidth in hertz over which you are measuring the noise. That last term matters because thermal noise is spread evenly across frequency, often called white noise, so the wider a range of frequencies your measurement includes, the more total noise energy it captures.

Here is a worked example. Take a 10,000 ohm (10 kΩ) resistor sitting at room temperature, using the standard reference temperature of 290 K, about 17 degrees Celsius, and measure its noise over a 20,000 Hz (20 kHz) bandwidth, roughly the range of human hearing. First compute 4kT: 4 times 1.38 times 10 to the negative 23 equals 5.52 times 10 to the negative 23, and multiplying by 290 gives 1.6008 times 10 to the negative 20. Multiply by the resistance, 10,000 ohms: 1.6008 times 10 to the negative 20 times 10,000 equals 1.6008 times 10 to the negative 16. Multiply by the bandwidth, 20,000 Hz: 1.6008 times 10 to the negative 16 times 20,000 equals 3.2016 times 10 to the negative 12. Finally take the square root: sqrt(3.2016 times 10 to the negative 12) equals about 1.79 times 10 to the negative 6 volts, or 1.79 microvolts RMS.

That is a genuinely tiny voltage, but it is not zero, and it cannot be engineered away. Because R and B sit inside the square root, doubling either one increases the noise voltage, though only by a factor of about 1.41 rather than doubling it outright. This is exactly why low noise amplifier designs favor smaller value resistors in the most sensitive, earliest stages of a circuit, and why cooling matters in ultra sensitive instrumentation: lower T directly lowers the noise floor. This resistor's own thermal noise is only one ingredient in a real circuit's overall noise, which is the subject of the next chapter.
